items.title: Block container access to Hetzner metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254)

milestone.title: v0.4.0
milestone.description: Detection and hardening — external monitoring, SSH hardening, metadata endpoint exposure, resource labels, key cleanup, S3 credentials, MySQL TLS docs.

items.body:
## Summary (plan item 3.3)

The Hetzner instance metadata endpoint at `169.254.169.254` is readable from the host and (by default) from containers running on the host. user-data sent via cloud-init contains secrets (MySQL passwords, JWT key, enroll secret, WSTEP key). A compromised container could read these secrets from the metadata endpoint.

## Why

After boot, the metadata endpoint is no longer needed. Blocking container access to it prevents a compromised Fleet, MySQL, Redis, or Caddy container from reading the provisioning secrets.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A firewall rule or `iptables`/`nftables` rule blocks container network interfaces from reaching `169.254.169.254` after boot
- [ ] The host can still reach it during cloud-init (needed for bootstrapping)
- [ ] A container cannot reach the metadata endpoint: `podman run --rm curlimages/curl curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/user-data` returns an error or times out
- [ ] The exposure is documented in README or `docs/security.md` (even if partially mitigated)

## Note

Document in README that user-data secrets are readable from the host (this is inherent to cloud-init) and that the mitigation only covers container access.

items.title: fix(security): detect IPv4-compatible, SIIT, and NAT64 addresses in deep link risk classifier
items.body:
## Summary / 概述

Strengthens the deep link risk classifier (`classifyEndpoint` in `src/utils/deeplinkRisk.ts`) to detect private / sensitive endpoints encoded as IPv4-compatible IPv6 (RFC 4291), SIIT IPv4-translated (RFC 6052 / RFC 7915), and NAT64 well-known / local prefix (RFC 6052 / RFC 8215) addresses.

### Motivation / 动机
`new URL()` canonicalizes IPv6 hostnames into standard RFC 5952 form (e.g. `[::127.0.0.1]` -> `[::7f00:1]`, `[::169.254.169.254]` -> `[::a9fe:a9fe]`, `[::ffff:0:169.254.169.254]` -> `[::ffff:0:a9fe:a9fe]`, `[64:ff9b::169.254.169.254]` -> `[64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe]`).

Previously, `extractIpv4Octets()` only matched standard dotted-quad IPv4 strings and IPv4-mapped `^::ffff:([0-9a-f]{1,4}):([0-9a-f]{1,4})$`. As a result:
- IPv4-compatible addresses (e.g., `http://[::127.0.0.1]/` or `http://[::169.254.169.254]/`) were unparsed and returned `null`.
- SIIT IPv4-translated addresses (e.g., `http://[::ffff:0:169.254.169.254]/`) were unparsed and returned `null`.
- NAT64 well-known prefix addresses (e.g., `http://[64:ff9b::169.254.169.254]/`) were unparsed and returned `null`.

This allowed malicious deep links targeting local loopback services (Ollama, local proxies) or cloud metadata endpoints (AWS/GCP IMDS `169.254.169.254`) via standard IPv6 notations to bypass the `DeepLinkImportDialog` security warning.

This change extends `extractIpv4Octets()` to recognize both hex and dotted representations of these IPv6 transition mechanisms, correctly identifying internal/private targets while leaving public addresses intact.

## Related Issue / 关联 Issue

N/A

## Screenshots / 截图

| Before / 修改前 | After / 修改后 |
|---|---|
| Deep links using `[::169.254.169.254]` or `[64:ff9b::127.0.0.1]` bypassed the risk warning banner | Appropriately classified as `privateEndpoint` and flagged in `DeepLinkImportDialog` |

- [x] `pnpm format:check` passes / 通过代码格式检查
- [ ] `cargo clippy` passes (if Rust code changed) / 通过 Clippy 检查（如修改了 Rust 代码）

items.title: fix(network): external_host_connectivity requires a TCP connect; probe IMDS
items.body:
## Summary

`external_host_connectivity` was set whenever the DNS lookup for `google.com` returned an address, without any connection being attempted. A sandbox that resolves names but blocks egress was therefore reported as having egress.

This PR makes the finding require a completed TCP connect, and adds the cloud metadata service (`169.254.169.254`) as a second target so the README's guidance for it can actually fire.

## What's changed

- `google.com` is reported only when a TCP connect to one of its resolved IPs completes on 443 or 80. Each attempt is bounded at 3s and the target at 8s.
- `169.254.169.254` is reported when a TCP connect to it on port 80 completes. The connection is closed unused, so no HTTP request is sent and no credentials are fetched. It is probed whether or not DNS works, with its own 2s bound.
- The value is still a `[]string` of target names, in the order `google.com`, `169.254.169.254`.
- Lookup and dial are injectable on `NetworkTask`, so the unit tests need no network.
- The README describes both targets and what a metadata service hit does and does not prove.

## Testing

- `go test ./...` with and without cgo, `-race`, `go vet` and the Windows build.
- 11 unit tests for the network task and `TCPReachable`. Each was checked against a deliberate regression: DNS-only reporting, a dial that always succeeds, no timeout, the metadata service never dialled, gated on DNS, or reported without a connect.
- Two new e2e scripts under `tests/fingerprint/`, both run by `make e2etests`:
  - `egress_dns_only.sh` runs the probe in a no-network container whose `/etc/hosts` resolves `google.com`, and expects `[]`. It fails on `main`.
  - `egress_imds.sh` binds `169.254.169.254` to loopback in a no-network container, and expects the address while a listener is up and `[]` without one. It fails on `main`.

| Scenario | `main` | This PR |
|---|---|---|
| Real network | `["google.com"]` | `["google.com"]` |
| No network, `/etc/hosts` resolves google.com | `["google.com"]` | `[]` |
| No network, no DNS | `[]` | `[]` |
| Metadata service reachable | `[]` | `["169.254.169.254"]` |

## Behaviour changes

- Sandboxes whose only egress is `HTTP(S)_PROXY` now report no direct connectivity. The proxy finding still reports the proxy.
- Containers on cloud VMs will usually now report `169.254.169.254`. With IMDSv2 and a hop limit of 1 the connect succeeds but a token cannot be fetched; the README says so.
- An off-cloud scan takes about 1.7s longer, because the metadata address does not answer.

## Not covered

- Direct-IP egress to hosts other than the metadata service when DNS is blocked.
- Ports other than 443 and 80.
- Alibaba's `100.100.100.200` and the AWS IPv6 endpoint `fd00:ec2::254`. Each would be one more entry in the target list.

items.title: stormcos nodes can't reach cloudid: 169.254.169.254 on their lo is stormimds
items.body:
Found while mining glennswest/stormimds#9 (https://github.com/glennswest/stormimds/issues/9) and #8 (https://github.com/glennswest/stormimds/issues/8#issuecomment-5853052060).

cloudid reaches bare-metal hosts at `169.254.169.254` in two ways: the DST-NAT rule it manages on RouterOS (#1), and DHCP option 121 routing the address via the gateway. Neither works on a **stormcos node**. The stormblock initramfs puts `169.254.169.254/32` on the node's `lo`, and stormimds binds it, so the node and everything in its host network namespace get stormimds's answer. On dev.g8.lo, which is not a stormcos node, the address still routes `via 192.168.8.1` to cloudid, as intended.

What stops working on stormcos hosts: the SSH keys, user-data, and `cloudid-agent` refresh that cloudid serves bare metal. So does stormd's CloudID key refresh (https://github.com/glennswest/stormd/issues/30).

Which service should answer a bare-metal node is the owner's decision, in stormimds#9. This issue records the effect on cloudid's side, so that cloudid's docs and #3 (repointing the identity source) don't assume every host can reach it.

**Proposed resolution:** once stormimds#9 is decided, either say in the README that stormcos nodes are served by stormimds and not cloudid, or have stormcos nodes reach cloudid by its service address instead of the link-local one.

items.title: fix(imds): always PUT IMDSv2 token to 169.254.169.254
items.body:
## Problem

`ExAws.InstanceMetaTokenProvider` routes the IMDSv2 session-token PUT to the ECS task-role credentials endpoint (`169.254.170.2` + `AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_RELATIVE_URI`) whenever that environment variable is set — which is the case in every ECS task with a task IAM role.

That endpoint is a credentials-only GET interface; it does not issue IMDSv2 tokens ([SDK container credential provider docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdkref/latest/guide/feature-container-credentials.html)). Its response body gets cached as a bogus token, and every subsequent metadata GET — which `ExAws.InstanceMeta.request/3` correctly sends to `169.254.169.254` — fails with `401 Unauthorized`.

In practice this breaks any IMDS usage from ECS tasks on EC2 container instances with IMDSv2 required (e.g. `ExAws.InstanceMeta.instance_role/1`, or libraries like `libcluster_ec2` calling the EC2 API through ExAws). We hit this running an Elixir cluster on ECS-on-EC2 with host networking.

## Fix

The token PUT now always targets the real IMDS token endpoint, `http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token` ([EC2 IMDSv2 docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/instancedata-data-retrieval.html)). The ECS credentials endpoint is unaffected — it is served by the separate task-role credentials path, which needs no IMDS token.

Includes a regression test asserting the token PUT URL stays `169.254.169.254` when `AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_RELATIVE_URI` is set; it fails on main and passes with this change.

Checked: `mix format` (Elixir 1.19.5), `mix test` (98 tests, 0 failures, with local DynamoDB), `mix dialyzer` (0 errors).

items.title: Support additionalNTPSources in agent-config.yaml

labels.name: OCA Required
labels.description: At least one contributor does not have an approved Oracle Contributor Agreement.

items.body:
## Problem

Nothing in the stack configures time for cluster nodes.

On a connected cluster that is survivable — RHCOS falls back to public NTP pools. In a disconnected environment there is no reachable time source at all. Clocks drift, and once they drift far enough every TLS handshake in the cluster begins failing: certificate validation, kubelet to API server, image pulls from the mirror. The symptoms look like unrelated networking faults, which makes it an expensive problem to diagnose.

We lost time to exactly this in an air-gapped install before tracing it back to clock skew.

## Change

Adds an `additional_ntp_sources` input, emitted as `additionalNTPSources` in `agent-config.yaml`. The Agent-based Installer uses that field to configure chrony on every node at install time, so nodes have a time source from first boot rather than needing a day-2 MachineConfig.

```hcl
additional_ntp_sources = ["169.254.169.254"]
```

```yaml
# agent-config.yaml
additionalNTPSources:
- 169.254.169.254
```

## On the default

It defaults to `169.254.169.254` — the OCI instance metadata endpoint, which Oracle provides as an NTP service and which every instance can reach with no egress.

**This is a behaviour change for existing users:** clusters that previously had no explicit NTP configuration will now get this source. On OCI that seems like the right default rather than a surprise, since the endpoint is always present and `additionalNTPSources` adds to, rather than replaces, any sources already configured.

Happy to flip it to `[]` and make it opt-in if you would rather not change existing behaviour — say the word and I will push that.

## Notes

- `terraform validate` passes.
- The diff in `create-cluster/main.tf` is larger than the change: `terraform fmt` realigned the `=` column in that module block because the new variable name is longer than the existing keys.

items.title: fix(browser): re-check the url the browser landed on before snapshotting
items.body:
## Problem

`_do_navigate` validates only the URL the caller asked for. A redirect hop
can land on a private/link-local address (e.g. `169.254.169.254`, the cloud
metadata endpoint) that was never validated, and the snapshot of the page is
taken right after. The `url_safety` module documents this exact gap:
"validating only the original URL leaves the redirect hop unguarded".

## Fix

After the navigation completes, re-check the URL the browser actually landed
on (`result['url']`): if it is an http(s) URL different from the requested
one and private targets are not allowed, run it through the same
`_validate_url_safe` check and fail before snapshotting. When
`allow_private_targets` is on, or there is no redirect, behavior is
unchanged.

## Tests

New `tests/test_browser_navigate_redirect_recheck.py`:

1. a redirect to `169.254.169.254` fails with the validation error and takes
   no snapshot
2. a navigation without a redirect still snapshots
3. `allow_private_targets` skips the re-check

- before the fix: 1 failed / 2 passed
- after the fix: 3 passed

The browser test family stays green (7 passed, 5 skipped); ruff F-gate
clean on both changed files.

items.title: fix(remote): reject IPv6 transition addresses embedding private IPv4
items.body:
## What this fixes

`_validate_public_address` decided whether a remote-media host was safe with
`ipaddress.is_global`. That property describes the address you wrote down, not the
machine the packet reaches. CPython classifies IPv6 transition formats that carry an
internal IPv4 as globally routable, so the guard let them through:

```python
from instructor.v2.core import remote
remote._validate_public_url("http://[64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe]/latest/meta-data/")
# before: returns None (accepted)
```

On a host with NAT64/DNS64 routing, which covers IPv6-only AWS and GCP subnets and many
corporate and mobile networks, that request is delivered to `169.254.169.254` and the IAM
credentials behind it. Loopback and RFC1918 are reachable the same way.

Reachable from the public API, not just the internal helper:

```python
from instructor.v2.core.multimodal import Image
Image.from_url("http://[64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe]/x.png")   # accepted
```

## What was actually bypassable

I checked each transition format against the guard on `main` rather than assuming, since
`is_global` already blocks several of them:

| Address | Really reaches | On `main` |
|---|---|---|
| `64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe` | 169.254.169.254 metadata | **accepted** |
| `64:ff9b::7f00:1` | 127.0.0.1 | **accepted** |
| `64:ff9b::a00:1` | 10.0.0.1 | **accepted** |
| `::169.254.169.254` | 169.254.169.254 | **accepted** |
| `::ffff:169.254.169.254` | 169.254.169.254 | already blocked |
| `2002:a9fe:a9fe::` | 169.254.169.254 | already blocked |
| `64:ff9b:1:a9fe:a9:fe00::` | 169.254.169.254 | already blocked |

So four are live bypasses: the well-known NAT64 prefix and the deprecated IPv4-compatible
form. The rest are handled for uniformity, not because they were open.

## The fix

`_embedded_ipv4` unwraps the IPv4 a transition format carries, using CPython's own
`ipv4_mapped`, `sixtofour` and `teredo` plus explicit handling for the two NAT64 prefixes
(RFC 6052) and IPv4-compatible. `_validate_public_address` then holds the address and every
embedded IPv4 to the same public check.

Because the guard is the single chokepoint for the URL host, resolved addresses, the socket
peer and every redirect target, this closes all of those paths at once.

A wrapper around a **public** IPv4 stays allowed, so IPv6-only egress through NAT64 keeps
working:

```
64:ff9b::808:808   -> 8.8.8.8            still allowed
2606:4700:4700::1111                     still allowed
```

## Tests

Nine cases added to `tests/v2/test_remote_fetch.py`: seven transition formats that must be
rejected, both through `_validate_public_address` and `_validate_public_url`, and two
wrappers around public IPv4 that must keep working.

I verified the rejection test actually catches the bug by reverting only the fix and
re-running: the four live bypasses fail, the three already-blocked cases still pass.

```
fix reverted:  4 failed, 5 passed
fix restored:  35 passed   (whole file)
tests/v2:      1881 passed, 8 pre-existing failures unrelated to this change
               (same 8 fail on a clean checkout; missing optional genai/vertexai deps)
```

`ruff check` and `ruff format --check` are clean on both files.

Fixes #2659

items.title: fix(ledger): treat unparseable URLs as privacy-unsafe
items.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The action ledger privacy filter is supposed to reject private hosts in event text. A candidate that looks like a URL but fails `new URL` (invalid port such as `http://169.254.169.254:foo`) was treated as public, then stripped before host and IP scans. The same host in a valid URL or as a bare address was already rejected. That hole can let link-local and loopback addresses into the public ledger.

## Evidence

Live `node` import of `actionEvent` on the patched tree. Invalid-port private URLs now throw `privacy-unsafe event data`. A public GitHub Actions run URL still succeeds.

```console
$ node --input-type=module -e "import { actionEvent } from './test/ledger-fixtures.mjs'; ..."
EVENT_THROW http://169.254.169.254:foo action ledger event: contains privacy-unsafe event data
EVENT_THROW http://127.0.0.1:notaport action ledger event: contains privacy-unsafe event data
EVENT_THROW http://169.254.169.254:99999 action ledger event: contains privacy-unsafe event data
EVENT_THROW https://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data action ledger event: contains privacy-unsafe event data
EVENT_THROW 169.254.169.254 action ledger event: contains privacy-unsafe event data
EVENT_OK https://github.com/openclaw/clawsweeper/actions/runs/123
```

Before this patch the three invalid-port strings printed `EVENT_OK`.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Unparseable URL candidates no longer bypass the privacy filter. Invalid ports that embed 169.254.169.254 or 127.0.0.1 are rejected the same way as valid URLs to those hosts.
- **Real environment tested:** Windows 11, Node v24.19.0, patched `scripts/ledger-schema.mjs` on branch `fix/privacy-url-fail-closed`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** From the patched checkout, ran `node --input-type=module` importing `actionEvent` with status strings `http://169.254.169.254:foo`, `http://127.0.0.1:notaport`, `http://169.254.169.254:99999`, plus the already-rejected valid metadata URL and a public GitHub run URL.
- **Evidence after fix:** terminal output from that `node` command (see Evidence). Invalid-port private URLs print `EVENT_THROW` with `privacy-unsafe event data`. `https://github.com/openclaw/clawsweeper/actions/runs/123` prints `EVENT_OK`.
- **Observed result after fix:** `privateUrl` fails closed when `new URL` throws, so those strings never reach the strip-then-scan path that previously hid the private IP.
- **What was not tested:** Publishing a crafted shard onto the live `state` branch.

## Change

`privateUrl` in `scripts/ledger-schema.mjs` returns true when URL parsing throws, instead of false.

## Origin

Introduced in [`7964f2af5f7`](https://github.com/openclaw/clawsweeper-state/commit/7964f2af5f7).

items.title: fix: prevent SSRF in webhook URL validation
items.body:
## What

The existing `assertUrlAllowed()` only inspected the **hostname text** before dispatching webhook/Slack alert requests. This is insufficient and bypassed by:

1. **DNS rebinding** — attacker controls DNS for `attacker.com`, which initially resolves to a public IP (passes text check), then at dispatch time resolves to `127.0.0.1` or `169.254.169.254`.
2. **HTTP redirects** — `attacker.com/redirect` returns `301 → http://169.254.169.254/` and `fetch()` followed it silently.

## Fixes

- **`isPrivateIp(ip)`** — new helper covering all private/loopback/link-local ranges for both IPv4 and IPv6, including IPv4-mapped IPv6 (`::ffff:127.0.0.1`).
- **`assertUrlAllowedAsync(url)`** — async version that resolves hostname to actual IPs via `dns.resolve4()` + `dns.resolve6()` and rejects any private address. Called at dispatch time.
- **`redirect: 'error'`** added to both `fetch()` calls in `sendSlackAlert` and `sendWebhookAlert` — redirects are now a hard error.
- Original synchronous `assertUrlAllowed()` preserved for config-save-time validation.

## Tests added (30 new)

Full coverage of sync text check, `isPrivateIp` ranges, and async DNS-rebinding scenarios.

## Files changed

- `server/src/api/alerts.ts`
- `server/test/alerts.test.ts`

items.title: [Yun Tianming] backend/src/server.ts: /functions/:slug proxy lets a slug rewrite the upstream host (unauthenticated SSRF)
items.body:
**Location:** `backend/src/server.ts:258-287`, `app.all('/functions/:slug', ...)`.

**Kind:** SSRF plus credential forwarding, on a route with no auth middleware.

**Evidence:** Express decodes `%2F` in route params after matching, so `GET /functions/%2F%2F169.254.169.254` yields `slug = '//169.254.169.254'`. The handler builds `new URL(`/${slug}`, baseUrl)`; verified here with node: `new URL('/' + '//evil.com', 'http://localhost:7133').href === 'http://evil.com/'` and `new URL('/' + '//169.254.169.254/latest', 'https://x.deno.dev').href === 'https://169.254.169.254/latest'`. The handler then forwards every string request header (including `authorization`, `cookie`, `x-api-key`) and the JSON body with the caller's method to that host, and returns the upstream body with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`.

**Impact:** any unauthenticated caller can make the backend issue arbitrary-method requests to internal addresses (cloud metadata, Postgres/PostgREST, Docker-adjacent services) and read the response, and can exfiltrate any credentials a legitimate client sends on this path.

**Fix would touch:** `server.ts` only. Validate `slug` against the function-slug grammar (e.g. `/^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$/`) before building the URL, or build with `encodeURIComponent(slug)` and assert `targetUrl.origin === new URL(baseUrl).origin`; consider whether the legacy proxy should require the same auth as `/api/functions`.

## Task Specification: RL-024
- **Task ID:** RL-024
- **Milestone:** M5: Custom Script Execution
- **Priority:** P0 (Blocker)
- **Responsible Role:** Dev 3 (Security Engine & Sandboxes)
- **Dependencies:** RL-022
- **Status:** Backlog

### Description & Technical Scope
Configure network namespace isolation ensuring script sandboxes have zero access to host interfaces, internal network subnets, or public internet unless explicitly permitted.

### Implementation Steps
1. Execute containers with `--network none` by default.
2. For simulated networking, bind container to an isolated internal Docker bridge with strict iptables rules.
3. Drop all egress traffic to link-local metadata addresses (`169.254.169.254`).
4. Block access to host loopback (`127.0.0.1`) and host LAN.

### Acceptance Criteria (Testable Statements)
- [ ] Scripts cannot reach `169.254.169.254` (cloud metadata service).
- [ ] Scripts cannot ping or connect to host machine ports.
- [ ] DNS requests to external domains fail immediately unless simulation explicitly enables mock gateway.

### Verification Instructions
```bash
cd backend && python3 -m pytest tests/test_sandbox_network.py -v
```

### Required Evidence
- [ ] Pytest test log verifying network egress blockage
- [ ] Packet capture log proving 169.254.169.254 drop

### Security Considerations
Critical defense against cloud credential exfiltration (SSRF to AWS IMDS).

items.title: Instance metadata reports the availability zone as the region (us-west-1-az2)
items.body:
> Filed by Claude (Opus 5.5), an AI agent, acting on behalf of Andy Fitzsimon, who owns this GitHub account and asked me to report what I found while testing [Lolly](https://github.com/lolly-tools/lolly) against a Spinifex sandbox. Andy did not review this text before it was posted; replies here reach him.

### Component

EC2 / instances

### Spinifex version

spx3.com sandbox (version not visible to me); code references are to `main` at fbf76cb (2026-10-26)

### What happened

On an instance in `us-west-1`, the metadata service reports the availability zone where the region belongs:

```shell
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X PUT http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 300")
curl -s -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/placement/region
# us-west-1-az2   (expected us-west-1)
curl -s -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" http://169.254.169.254/latest/dynamic/instance-identity/document
# "region": "us-west-1-az2", "availabilityZone": "us-west-1-az2"
```

`regionFromAZ` in `spinifex/domains/ec2/guestmetadata/metadata.go:760` strips one trailing letter, which fits AWS zone names like `us-west-1a`. This deployment names zones `us-west-1-az2`, so the zone comes back unchanged as the region.

**Why it matters.** AWS SDKs and tools take their default region from these two fields (the identity document and `placement/region`). Software on an instance then signs requests for region `us-west-1-az2` and talks to the wrong endpoint, or gets signature errors. Using the node's configured region, instead of deriving it from the zone name, would avoid depending on the naming scheme.

items.title: [rpc-validation] Host guard runs only for http: — https:// loopback / link-local / cloud-metadata RPC URLs pass validation (SSRF)
items.body:
## Summary

`normalizeRpcUrl()` applies the loopback / private-LAN rejection **only to `http:` URLs**. Any `https:` URL passes regardless of host, so `https://127.0.0.1:2375`, `https://169.254.169.254/…`, `https://[::1]:8545` and `https://kubernetes.default.svc/` are all accepted as a custom RPC endpoint. `setRpcOverride()` additionally accepts an arbitrary URL with no validation at all.

## Evidence (source)

`src/rpc-validation.ts:106-122`:

```ts
const insecure = parsed.protocol === 'http:';
let note: string | undefined;
if (insecure) {
  if (isLoopbackHost(parsed.hostname)) { ... }
  else if (isPrivateLanHost(parsed.hostname)) { ... }
  else { return { ok: false, error: 'Use https:// for this address. ...' }; }
}
const path = parsed.pathname.replace(/\/+$/, '');
const url = `${parsed.protocol}//${parsed.host}${path}`;
return { ok: true, url, origin: ..., host: parsed.host, insecure, note };
```

The whole host check lives inside `if (insecure)` — for `https:` execution falls straight through to `return { ok: true }`. There is no host allowlist on the https path (the only earlier checks are protocol, credentials, query/hash — `:95-104`).

Additionally `isPrivateLanHost()` (`:59-72`) classifies **`169.254.0.0/16` as "local network"**:

```ts
if (a === 169 && b === 254) return true;   // link-local, treated as LAN
```

so plain `http://169.254.169.254/` is *explicitly permitted* (it only gets the "local network" note at `:118`) — that is the cloud instance-metadata address.

Verified against the shipped code with a local harness (no third-party hosts were contacted):

```
PASS  https://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/    (cloud metadata)
PASS  https://127.0.0.1:2375/                        (loopback)
PASS  https://[::1]:8545/
PASS  https://kubernetes.default.svc/
```

`src/client.ts:80-86` (`setRpcOverride`) is worse — it stores the value without calling `normalizeRpcUrl` at all. The README (`:118-121`) advertises the package for back-end/wallet-service use, i.e. a server that accepts a user-supplied RPC URL becomes an SSRF pivot.

Note the guard is also **hostname-string based**, so a public hostname that resolves to `127.0.0.1` (or a DNS-rebinding pair) bypasses it even on `http:`.

## Reproduction

```js
import { normalizeRpcUrl } from './src/rpc-validation';
normalizeRpcUrl('https://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/')  // { ok: true, ... }
normalizeRpcUrl('http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/')   // { ok: true, note: 'Plain http only works on your local network…' }
normalizeRpcUrl('http://10.0.0.5:8545')                       // { ok: true }  (by design for LAN)
```

## Impact

Server-side request forgery / port-scanning / metadata-theft primitive wherever the SDK runs with a user-provided RPC URL: read the instance metadata (IAM credentials on EC2/GCP), reach internal services (`127.0.0.1:2375` Docker API, cluster-internal DNS names), or distinguish open/closed ports from timing/errors — in the browser it also becomes a localhost port-scan oracle for a visited page.

## Suggested fix

- Reject loopback / private / link-local / CGNAT / IPv6 ULA hosts **regardless of scheme** (and re-check after DNS resolution, or on the resolved IP, to defeat rebinding).
- Treat `169.254.0.0/16` as forbidden metadata space, not "LAN".
- Route `setRpcOverride` through `normalizeRpcUrl` too (fail closed).

---
Reporting account (airdrop username): **apienz_ase**

Hunt Watch was searching IOCs that intel adjudication had already rejected, and file hashes never went through semantic review so bunk commit SHAs could land as discriminating and get hunted.

This PR does both sides of that fix:
1. Hashes join the URL/domain semantic adjudication path (context window, candidate check, prompt guidance). A hash a failed or over-budget batch never reviews is stored `deferred_unreviewed` and is neither promoted nor hunted until re-enrichment.
2. Hunt eligibility matches promote: only `discriminating` / `contextual` / `uncertain` (and legacy untiered IOCs) are searched. Excluded values are counted, narrated, kept out of Tier 2 generation, and never allowed to ground a Tier 2 query (a `reference` value may still narrow a query that another artifact grounds). The threat report card follows the same split.

## Behavior change

Hashes now share the URL/domain failure path. Deferred is "not yet reviewed," not rejection. Already-enriched reports keep stored tiers until re-enriched; `reference` / `denied` stop being hunted as soon as this lands. Only `reference` and deferred values go on the Tier 2 denylist and into the narrative count; `denied` is an extraction verdict on the IOC kind (`install.sh` seen as a domain), so Tier 2 may still filter on those strings. Only hashes found in prose (`hash_high_entropy`) go to model review; a hash under an IOC heading (`ioc_section`) or written defanged (`defanged_source`) is attributed by its placement and stays deterministic. Prose hashes compete with URLs and domains for the 900-candidate review budget in document order. In Tier 2, a `reference` value can narrow a query that another artifact grounds but cannot be what grounds it.

## To test

Local Kibana with a GenAI connector for AlertZero, threat-intel supply enabled (or at least the enrich workflow enabled), and some endpoint (or other) logs so Tier 1/2 have an index universe. Examples below assume `KBN=http://localhost:5601/kbn` and `AUTH=elastic:changeme`.

Researchers describe a vulnerable PHP path. The commit that patched the vulnerabilities is {commit}.

'''

items.title: 🛡️ Sentinel: [CRITICAL] Fix Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in video downloader
items.body:
🚨 **Severity**: CRITICAL
💡 **Vulnerability**: The application was fetching download URLs from the external Cobalt API and blindly requesting those URLs with `requests.get`, which followed redirects by default. A compromised Cobalt server could redirect requests to the internal network (e.g. 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254), resulting in a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF).
🎯 **Impact**: A malicious actor could exploit this vulnerability to probe internal services or perform metadata retrieval attacks on cloud environments.
🔧 **Fix**: Implemented strict IP validation (`is_safe_url`) using `socket.getaddrinfo` to resolve and check against loopback, private, link-local, multicast, and unspecified ranges. Configured `requests.get` with `allow_redirects=False` to securely inspect and validate every domain in a redirect chain prior to forwarding the request, avoiding DNS rebinding or direct redirect exploits.
✅ **Verification**: Validated functionality against common internal IPs (127.0.0.1, localhost, 169.254.169.254) using a targeted test script while preserving standard internet request flows, passing the test suite via `python manage.py test`.

items.body:
## Summary

- `isSafeUrl()` checked the initial URL only; a public host that responded with a redirect to `169.254.169.254` (or any other private/internal address) bypassed the guard because Node's `fetch` follows redirects transparently
- Added `safeFetch()` to `src/lib/isSafeUrl.ts` — a drop-in replacement that uses `redirect: 'manual'`, validates every `Location` header with `isSafeUrl`, resolves relative redirects, and caps at 5 hops
- Updated `scrapeWithFetch()` in `/api/scrape/route.ts` and the direct `fetch` in `/api/projects/[id]/scrape/route.ts` to use `safeFetch`

items.title: aws-network-policy-agent egress port-scoping bug
items.body:
TCP NetworkPolicy egress rules whose peer is 0.0.0.0/0 appear to have their port restriction ignored by **aws-network-policy-agent**. Once a rule like this exists in a policy, connections succeed on **any TCP port to any IPv4 destination**, not just the ports declared in the rule. The rule's own except exclusion (e.g. excluding the IMDS address) is also not honored — traffic to the excluded IP still gets through.

---
**Policy under test (minimal reproduction)**

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: repro-netpol
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: repro
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 0.0.0.0/0
            except:
              - 169.254.169.254/32
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 443
```

---

**Expected behavior**

- TCP to any IPv4 (except 169.254.169.254) on port 443 only: allowed.
- TCP to any IPv4 on any other port: blocked.
- TCP to 169.254.169.254 on port 443: blocked (excluded by except).

---
**Actual behavior**

- TCP to any port on any IPv4 destination is allowed, including:
- 169.254.169.254:443 — the address the rule explicitly excepts.
- 169.254.169.254:80 — no rule permits port 80 to this address at all.
- Arbitrary public IPs on arbitrary ports never declared in any rule (e.g. :80, :22).
- Other pods in-cluster (any namespace) on ports never declared in any rule — because 0.0.0.0/0 matches by IP only and includes cluster-internal RFC1918 addresses too.

---

**Reproduction / evidence**
From inside a pod matched by the policy above, using only stdlib socket.create_connection() (bypasses any userspace HTTP semantics, pure TCP handshake test):


Destination:port | Rule that should apply | Expected | Actual
-- | -- | -- | --
169.254.169.254:443 | excepted from the 443 rule | blocked | connects
169.254.169.254:80 | no rule permits port 80 to this IP | blocked | connects
<public IP>:80 | only port 443 is declared | blocked | connects
<public IP>:22 | only port 443 is declared | blocked | connects
<in-cluster pod IP>:8080 | no rule matches this pod/port | blocked | connects
<public IP>:443 | port 443 declared | reachable | connects (correct)

**Confirmed:**

- Reproduces with a single 0.0.0.0/0-keyed TCP rule present — not only when multiple rules share that peer.
- Reproduces identically across multiple pod instances and multiple underlying nodes — not instance- or node-specific.
- The leaked traffic is confirmed to actually leave the pod's network namespace (verified via TCP handshake completing against real, independently-verified endpoints) — this is not a false positive from a bypassed test path (we did not use kubectl exec/port-forward, which don't cross the pod's veth).

The following curls returned "Established Connection", evidence that at least handshake occurs.

``` shell
# IMDS excepted-port leak
curl -v --connect-timeout 4 --max-time 5 -o /dev/null http://169.254.169.254:443/
# IMDS wrong-port leak
curl -v --connect-timeout 4 --max-time 5 -o /dev/null http://169.254.169.254:80/
#  Public IP wrong-port leak
curl -v --connect-timeout 4 --max-time 5 -o /dev/null http://1.1.1.1:80/
# Same-namespace pod, no matching rule
curl -v --connect-timeout 4 --max-time 5 -o /dev/null http://10.79.59.173:8080/
# Second public IP, wrong port
curl -v --connect-timeout 4 --max-time 5 -o /dev/null http://8.8.8.8:22/
#  OTLP host, wrong port
curl -v --connect-timeout 4 --max-time 5 -o /dev/null http://obs-instrumentation-collector.system-observability-service.svc.cluster:9999
```

---

**Why this matters**
- The IMDS except failure is the most serious instance: a policy explicitly written to keep a pod from reaching instance metadata does not actually do so, once any 0.0.0.0/0-keyed TCP rule exists in that policy.


**Please:**

- Confirm whether this is a known issue / has a tracking ticket.
- If not reproducible as described, happy to provide the full test script and raw output.

items.title: fix(gitspace): apply the network policy to devcontainer feature downloads
items.body:
Part of #3687 (the SSRF half; the tar-slip half is #3729).

### Problem

Devcontainer feature sources come from the repository's `devcontainer.json`, but the server fetches them with no restriction on where they point:

- tarball features use a bare `http.Get(url)` (with `nolint:gosec,noctx`), and the only check on the URL is that it's http(s) and ends in `.tgz`;
- OCI features use oras' default client, so a reference like `169.254.169.254/feature:1` makes the server call `https://169.254.169.254/v2/...`.

So anyone who can push a `devcontainer.json` and start a gitspace can make the server connect to loopback, private and link-local addresses, including the cloud metadata endpoint. Redirects are followed too.

### Fix

Both downloads now go through one transport whose dialer enforces the shared `netpolicy` from `net.Dialer.Control`, the same way repository import does (`importer.newBaseTransport`). Because the check runs on each resolved address right before connect, it also covers redirects and DNS answers that change after a lookup, and a rejected address is never contacted.

- `utils.NewFeatureDownloadTransport(policy)` builds the transport. It's passed from `EmbeddedDockerOrchestrator` through `InstallFeatures` → `DownloadFeatures` → `downloadFeature`.
- Tarball: `http.NewRequestWithContext` + a client on that transport, so the request also respects cancellation now.
- OCI: the repository gets an `auth.Client` matching `auth.DefaultClient` (same header, cache and retry behaviour), but on top of the restricted transport.
- New config, all defaulting to `false` like the importer and webhook settings: `GITNESS_GITSPACE_FEATURES_ALLOW_PRIVATE_NETWORK`, `GITNESS_GITSPACE_FEATURES_ALLOW_LOOPBACK`, `GITNESS_GITSPACE_FEATURES_ALLOW_LINK_LOCAL`. These are for setups that host features on an internal server or registry.

Public sources are unaffected. I pulled `ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/common-utils:2` through the new transport to check the anonymous token flow still works.

### Tests

`app/gitspace/orchestrator/utils/feature_download_transport_test.go` runs a loopback `httptest` server as the "internal" host. By default the download fails with `netpolicy.ErrAddressNotAllowed` and the server is never hit. With `AllowLoopback`, the download goes through and the file is written. I also checked by hand that OCI references to `localhost` and `169.254.169.254` are refused with the same error.

```
go test ./netpolicy/ ./app/gitspace/orchestrator/...   # ok
go build ./cmd/gitness                                  # ok
```

This touches a different part of `types/config.go` and `wire_gen.go` than #3732, so the two shouldn't conflict.

items.title: Allow GKE metadata server egress for the GCP MCP addon with Workload Identity
items.body:
## Problem

The GCP addon NetworkPolicy allows egress to `0.0.0.0/0` except `169.254.169.254/32`. On GKE with Workload Identity, that address *is* how pods get credentials: the GKE metadata server serves the KSA's Google identity there.

- **Without Dataplane V2:** requests are redirected to `169.254.169.252:988` before the policy is evaluated. The `0.0.0.0/0` rule allows that, so the addon works.
- **With Dataplane V2** (and therefore on every Autopilot cluster): the policy sees the original `169.254.169.254:80` and drops it. The images authenticate through Application Default Credentials (`observability-mcp` has no key file and no credential config), so credential lookup hangs and every tool call times out with no error in the pod log.

GKE's [network policy docs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/network-policy) say Dataplane V2 clusters must allow egress to `169.254.169.254/32` on ports 80 and 8080 for Workload Identity.

## Fix

Add that egress rule when the addon is configured for Workload Identity: `workloadIdentity.enabled: true`, or the KSA has the `iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account` annotation (the values the GKE Workload Identity docs page tells users to set). The existing `except` stays, so the policy is unchanged for key-file setups and for anyone not using Workload Identity. The node's credentials stay blocked there.

On a `GKE_METADATA` node pool, the metadata server only issues the pod's own Workload Identity token, never the node service account's, so opening it adds no access beyond what the KSA is already bound to.

## Testing

Ran `helm template` on the GCP addon NetworkPolicy:

| Values | Metadata rule rendered |
|---|---|
| defaults (`gcp.enabled`) | no (output identical to master) |
| `iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account` annotation only | yes |
| `workloadIdentity.enabled: true` only | yes |
| `serviceAccount.annotations: null` | no, renders cleanly |
| annotation with empty value / unrelated annotation | no |
| `networkPolicy.enabled: false` | no policy |

Also ran `helm lint` (clean) and `kubectl apply --dry-run=client` on the rendered policy.

items.title: fix(cli): validate every http_fetch redirect target
items.body:
## Problem

`http_fetch` validated only the **initial** URL, then called `fetch()` with its default `redirect: 'follow'`:

```ts
const response = await fetch(parsed.toString(), { method, headers, ... });
```

A public URL could therefore return `302 Location: http://127.0.0.1/...`, `http://169.254.169.254/...`, or `file:///...` and fetch would follow it **after** the allowlist check. That is a post-validation SSRF escalation. This is the redirect finding explicitly carried forward from #4503 / #4504 (the IPv4-mapped IPv6 fix landed in #4504).

## Change

Follow redirects manually:

- `redirect: 'manual'`, max **10** hops.
- Run `validateUrl()` on every `Location` before issuing the next request; relative locations resolve against the current URL.
- Cancel each redirect response body before following.
- Drop `Authorization`, `Cookie`, and `Proxy-Authorization` when the redirect crosses origins.
- Match fetch's method rules: `303` becomes GET except for GET/HEAD; `301/302` rewrite POST to GET; `307/308` preserve method and body.
- Report the final validated URL in `result.url`.
- Blocked redirects return the same codes as initial-URL rejections (`PRIVATE_ADDRESS`, `FORBIDDEN_PROTOCOL`); the hop cap returns `REDIRECT_LIMIT`.

## Regression tests

`http-fetch-redirect-ssrf.test.ts` mocks `fetch()` and covers:

1. public → `http://127.0.0.1/...` blocked with no second request;
2. public → IPv4-mapped metadata (`[::ffff:169.254.169.254]`) blocked;
3. public → `file:///etc/passwd` blocked;
4. public relative redirect followed; final status/body/URL correct;
5. cross-origin redirect drops `Authorization`;
6. redirect loop stops at `REDIRECT_LIMIT` after 11 fetches.

Baseline (source stashed, tests kept):

- all six fail — the baseline returns the 302 as a successful result and never validates the target.

Candidate:

- new tests **6/6 passed**;
- existing http-fetch suite + new tests: **43/43 passed**;
- `tsc --noEmit` reports no errors in the changed file;
- no BOM/U+FFFD; `git diff --check` clean.

## Compatibility

- Initial-URL validation and header sanitization are unchanged.
- Public redirects still follow, up to 10 hops; the final URL is now reported.
- The only behavioral restriction is the intended one: every redirect hop must pass the same allowlist.

items.title: Sécurité : une IPv4 mappée en IPv6 contournait la défense anti-SSRF
items.body:
Corrige le défaut signalé par **@zaderlyl** — le `todo` de #134 peut être retiré une fois ceci fusionné.

## Le défaut

Une IPv4 mappée en IPv6 s'écrit de deux façons :

```
::ffff:127.0.0.1   la forme pointée, celle qu'on tape
::ffff:7f00:1      la forme hexadécimale, celle que new URL écrit APRÈS normalisation
```

`ipIsPrivate` ne reconnaissait que la première. Or le contrôleur ne voit jamais que la seconde :

```js
new URL('http://[::ffff:169.254.169.254]/').hostname
// → '[::ffff:a9fe:a9fe]'
```

`a9fe:a9fe`, c'est **169.254.169.254** — les métadonnées cloud. Elle passait pour une adresse publique, et le proxy acceptait d'aller la chercher depuis le réseau du hub.

Vérifié avant correction en rejouant la fonction telle qu'elle était : `::ffff:7f00:1`, `::ffff:a9fe:a9fe` et `::ffff:a00:1` rendaient toutes les trois `false`.

## Portée réelle

Je préfère la dire exactement plutôt que de la dramatiser : la liste blanche de domaines bloque en amont, donc le contournement demandait `IMG_PROXY_OPEN=1`, ou un hôte autorisé dont l'enregistrement AAAA pointe vers une telle adresse. **Ce n'est pas exploitable sur une installation par défaut.** Ça restait un trou dans la défense qui est précisément là pour ce cas.

## La correction

Reconstruire l'IPv4 à partir des deux groupes hexadécimaux, et la soumettre au même examen que n'importe quelle IPv4.

Le **piège inverse** est testé aussi : `::ffff:5db8:d822` (93.184.216.34) doit **rester publique**, sinon le proxy se coupe de sources légitimes servies en IPv4 via une pile v6.

Ce qui embarque de l'IPv4 sans être déchiffrable sans risque — NAT64 `64:ff9b::`, formes compressées exotiques — est refusé comme un format inconnu. Un proxy de planches n'a aucune raison d'aller chercher une image derrière un NAT64.

## Tests

14 tests, dont **9 échouent contre le code d'avant**. Le dernier vérifie le maillon qui explique tout : que c'est bien la forme normalisée par `new URL` qui arrive au contrôle, et non celle qu'on écrit.

items.title: [New Rule] Discovery Commands Followed by Instance Metadata Service Access
items.body:
## Summary - What I changed

- Adds a medium-severity cross-platform ES|QL rule that correlates multiple discovery commands with access to the cloud instance metadata service (IMDS) from the same process tree.
- Covers Linux, macOS and Windows discovery utilities, plus connections to `169.254.169.254`.
- Detects post-exploitation activity in which a compromised process enumerates the host and then queries IMDS for instance details or temporary role credentials.

## Description

After gaining code execution attackers commonly run a burst of host, user, and network discovery commands (`whoami`, `uname`, `ip`, `systeminfo`, `sw_vers`, ...). Each step on its own is common and noisy; together, from the same process tree within a few seconds, they form a much stronger signal.

The rule groups discovery executions by their parent process (`process.parent.entity_id`) and IMDS network events by both the connecting process and its parent (`process.entity_id` and `process.parent.entity_id`). This covers a shell that runs discovery commands followed by `curl`/`wget`, as well as a script interpreter (Python, Node, PowerShell) that spawns discovery tools and queries IMDS itself. An alert fires when a single process tree runs at least 3 distinct discovery commands, accesses IMDS at least once, and all matching activity falls within 10 seconds.

The rule excludes a small set of parent executables known to legitimately combine discovery and metadata access (Jamf, Homebrew, Puppet, Chef, Google Cloud SDK, Docker Desktop). 

## How To Test

Validate the rule:

    python -m detection_rules validate-rule rules/cross-platform/discovery_commands_followed_by_imds_access.toml

Validate TOML formatting:

    python -m detection_rules toml-lint -f rules/cross-platform/discovery_commands_followed_by_imds_access.toml

Validate attack:

- Linux / macOS: `whoami; uname -a; hostname; ip a 2>/dev/null || ifconfig; curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`

### What is the issue?

`readVMUserData` and `getEC2MetadataToken` in `ipn/conffile/cloudconf.go` use `http.DefaultClient` with no timeout and no context deadline. Each metadata request fails after a few seconds.

Linux.

items.title: [Bug] Webhook SSRF via IPv4-Compatible IPv6 Bypass in isPrivateUrl (RFC 4291)
items.body:
### Issue Description

In `packages/lib/server-only/webhooks/is-private-url.ts`, private address validation checks for loopback, RFC 1918, link-local, and IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses (the latter fixed in #2901).

However, **IPv4-compatible IPv6 addresses** (RFC 4291 §2.5.5.1, e.g. `http://[::127.0.0.1]` or `http://[::169.254.169.254]`) are not decoded, allowing webhooks to bypass SSRF validation and target private loopback or cloud metadata services.

#### Root Cause:
1. When a URL like `http://[::127.0.0.1]:3000/` or `http://[::169.254.169.254]/` is parsed by `new URL()`, Node.js normalizes the dotted IPv4-compatible notation to hexadecimal notation:
   - `::127.0.0.1` -> `::7f00:1`
   - `::169.254.169.254` -> `::a9fe:a9fe`
   - `::10.0.0.1` -> `::a00:1`
   - `::192.168.1.1` -> `::c0a8:101`
2. `isPrivateUrl` checks `ZIpSchema.safeParse(normalizedHost)`, which succeeds because `::7f00:1` is a valid IPv6 address.
3. The IPv4-mapped hex decoder (`v4MappedHex`) only matches `^::ffff:...`. Because IPv4-compatible addresses start with `::` rather than `::ffff:`, they slip past:
   - Not caught by `startsWith('127.')`
   - Not caught by `normalizedHost === '::1'`
   - Not caught by `^::ffff:...`
   - `isPrivateUrl` returns `false`.
4. In `assertNotPrivateUrl` (`assert-webhook-url.ts:105`):
   ```typescript
   if (hostname.length === 0 || ZIpSchema.safeParse(hostname).success) {
     return;
   }
   ```
   Because `hostname` is recognized as a valid IP literal, it returns immediately and skips DNS resolution. The private webhook request is permitted and dispatched.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Test `isPrivateUrl` with an IPv4-compatible address:
   ```ts
   import { isPrivateUrl } from '@documenso/lib/server-only/webhooks/is-private-url';

   // Control (caught correctly)
   console.log(isPrivateUrl('http://127.0.0.1')); // true
   console.log(isPrivateUrl('http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]')); // true (fixed in #2901)

   // Bypass (IPv4-compatible IPv6)
   console.log(isPrivateUrl('http://[::127.0.0.1]:3000')); // returns FALSE (Expected: true)
   console.log(isPrivateUrl('http://[::169.254.169.254]')); // returns FALSE (Expected: true)
   console.log(isPrivateUrl('http://[::10.0.0.1]')); // returns FALSE (Expected: true)
   ```
2. In the UI or API (`webhook.createWebhook`), create a webhook pointing to `http://[::127.0.0.1]:3000/webhook` or `http://[::169.254.169.254]/latest/meta-data/`.
3. Notice `assertNotPrivateUrl` allows the webhook to be saved and dispatched.

### Expected Behavior

`isPrivateUrl` and `assertNotPrivateUrl` should reject all IPv4-compatible IPv6 addresses (`::/96`) mapping to private ranges (`::127.0.0.0/104`, `::10.0.0.0/104`, `::169.254.0.0/112`, etc.), in both dotted and hex normalized forms, returning `true` for `isPrivateUrl` and throwing `WEBHOOK_INVALID_REQUEST` in `assertNotPrivateUrl`.

### Current Behavior

- `http://127.0.0.1:3000` -> Blocked (Expected)
- `http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]:3000` -> Blocked (Expected)
- `http://[::127.0.0.1]:3000` -> **Allowed** (bypasses `isPrivateUrl` and `assertNotPrivateUrl`)
- `http://[::169.254.169.254]` -> **Allowed** (bypasses `isPrivateUrl` and `assertNotPrivateUrl`)

### Proposed Solution

Add IPv4-compatible IPv6 normalization (hex and dotted forms) in `is-private-url.ts`:
```typescript
// IPv4-compatible IPv6, dotted form (e.g. ::127.0.0.1)
const v4CompatDotted = normalizedHost.match(/^::(\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)$/i);

if (v4CompatDotted) {
  return isPrivateUrl(`http://${v4CompatDotted[1]}`);
}

// IPv4-compatible IPv6, hex form (e.g. ::7f00:1 or ::a9fe:a9fe)
const v4CompatHex = normalizedHost.match(/^::([0-9a-f]{1,4}):([0-9a-f]{1,4})$/i);

if (v4CompatHex) {
  const high = parseInt(v4CompatHex[1], 16);
  const low = parseInt(v4CompatHex[2], 16);
  const ipv4 = [high >> 8, high & 0xff, low >> 8, low & 0xff].join('.');

  return isPrivateUrl(`http://${ipv4}`);
}
```

I have the fix and unit test suite implemented and verified locally covering private loopback, RFC 1918, link-local, and public IPv4-compatible addresses. Happy to submit the pull request once reviewed by the team!

### Operating System

Windows 11 / Linux

### Browser

All

### Version

2.20.0 (commit `8724500`, main)

- On the DPU OS path, the agent's default FMDS address is `169.254.169.254/30` (`crates/host-support/src/agent_config.rs:425-433`), HBN gets the `169.254.169.253/30` gateway on `pf0dpu1_if` (`crates/agent/templates/nvue_startup_fnn.conf:33-42`), and `plan_fmds_armos_routing` builds routes from the interface's IPv4 address with `169.254.169.253` as the gateway (`crates/agent/src/main_loop.rs:1692-1725`). The TODO above it notes that FMDS still needs a documented IPv6 address (`crates/agent/src/main_loop.rs:1690-1691`).

#2401 added IPv6 addresses to the metadata FMDS returns, but an instance whose interface has only IPv6 can't reach FMDS to read them, or to get the machine identity tokens FMDS serves (`docs/getting-started/installation-options/day0-machine-identity.md:5`).

FMDS should have a documented IPv6 address that an instance can reach from an IPv6-only interface on both the DPF and DPU OS paths, while `169.254.169.254` keeps working.

## What this involves

- Choose the IPv6 FMDS address and how instances route to it. No doc page lists the IPv4 address either, so document both.
- Assign the IPv6 address on the FMDS interface alongside the IPv4 one, render the matching HBN address or route for FNN tenant ports, and install IPv6 reply routing in `setup_metadata_routing` and `plan_fmds_armos_routing`.
- Cover a metadata request from an IPv6-only tenant interface in the agent and FMDS tests, and keep the IPv4 address and routes unchanged.
- Remove the TODO at `crates/agent/src/main_loop.rs:1690-1691`.

items.title: url_guard allows IPv4-compatible, NAT64, 6to4 and trailing-dot forms of internal addresses
items.body:
## Problem

`url_guard.validate_fetch_url` blocks loopback, private and cloud-metadata IPv4 literals, and unwraps IPv4-mapped IPv6 (`::ffff:a.b.c.d`). It does not recognise the other IPv6 forms that embed an IPv4 address, or an IPv4 literal written with a trailing dot. These URLs are allowed:

| URL | Embedded address | Observed |
|---|---|---|
| `http://[::127.0.0.1]/` | IPv4-compatible, loopback | allowed |
| `http://[::169.254.169.254]/` | IPv4-compatible, metadata | allowed |
| `http://[64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe]/` | NAT64 well-known prefix, 169.254.169.254 | allowed |
| `http://[64:ff9b::a00:1]/` | NAT64, 10.0.0.1 | allowed |
| `http://[2002:a9fe:a9fe::]/` | 6to4, 169.254.169.254 | allowed |
| `http://127.0.0.1./` | trailing-dot IPv4 | allowed (treated as a DNS name) |
| `http://169.254.169.254./` | trailing-dot IPv4 | allowed |
| `http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]/` (control) | IPv4-mapped | blocked |
| `http://0177.0.0.1/` (control) | octal IPv4 | blocked |

Found in an October 2026 correctness audit. Reproduced on `main` at `10f5627` (the code is unchanged since v8.0.0).

## Reproduction

```python
from qwed_new.core.url_guard import validate_fetch_url

for url in ["http://[::127.0.0.1]/", "http://[64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe]/",
            "http://[2002:a9fe:a9fe::]/", "http://127.0.0.1./",
            "http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]/"]:
    try:
        validate_fetch_url(url)
        print("allowed", url)
    except ValueError as e:
        print("blocked", url, e)
```

## Cause

- `src/qwed_new/core/url_guard.py`, line 76: only `ipv4_mapped` is unwrapped. IPv4-compatible (`::/96`), NAT64 (`64:ff9b::/96`, RFC 6052) and 6to4 (`2002::/16`, `addr.sixtofour`) are not, and none of these prefixes is in `_LOCAL_NETWORKS`.
- Line 147: a host that does not parse as an IP literal is returned as a name. `127.0.0.1.` fails `ipaddress.ip_address` because of the trailing dot, so it is never checked as an address, although many resolvers and the WHATWG URL parser treat it as `127.0.0.1`.

## Impact

Low. The only callers are operator-controlled: `SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL` from the environment (`core/alerting.py`) and `qwed provider import <url>` (`providers/config_manager.py`, https only). No API route passes untrusted input to it. Reachability of the IPv6 forms also depends on the network (NAT64 or 6to4 gateways; IPv4-compatible addresses are deprecated and rarely routed). This is defence-in-depth hardening, so the guard matches its own description.

## Fix direction

- Unwrap IPv4-compatible, NAT64 well-known-prefix and 6to4 addresses to their IPv4 part and judge that, as is already done for v4-mapped. Also add `64:ff9b:1::/48` (local-use NAT64).
- Strip a single trailing dot from the host before the literal-IP check.
- Optionally block `::/96`, `64:ff9b::/96` and `2002::/16` outright, since none is a normal destination for these sinks.

## Regression tests

Every URL in the table above must be blocked; a public IPv6 address and a normal hostname must still be allowed.

Extensions had no way to call outside services or hold an API key. Now an extension declares hosts with `defineNetwork` and secret names with `defineSecrets`. The owner approves both at install and sets secret values in Settings.

items.body:
## What happens
The debug proxy's CONNECT tunnel handler explicitly disables the socket timeout for the tunnel lifetime (`upstreamSocket.setTimeout(0)`) and applies no target restriction, idle timeout, or connection limit. A connected client can open unbounded tunnels to arbitrary internal hosts (including cloud metadata endpoints like `169.254.169.254`) and hold them open indefinitely, exhausting Gateway file descriptors and pivoting into internal networks.

## File affected
- `src/proxy-capture/proxy-server.ts:420-431`

## Vulnerable code
```typescript
// src/proxy-capture/proxy-server.ts:420-431
const upstreamSocket = net.connect(port, hostname, () => {
  // This inactivity timeout only protects opening the upstream socket. CONNECT
  // tunnels are intentionally long-lived and must not inherit it.
  upstreamSocket.setTimeout(0);   // <-- disables timeout entirely
  upstreamSocket.off("timeout", onUpstreamConnectTimeout);
  clientSocket.write("HTTP/1.1 200 Connection Established\r\n\r\n");
  ...
  clientSocket.pipe(upstreamSocket);
  upstreamSocket.pipe(clientSocket);
});
```

No per-tunnel idle timeout, no maximum tunnel count per client, no allowlist on `hostname:port`. The only gate is the env-bypassable `assertDebugProxyDirectUpstreamAllowed()`.

## Impact
- **Severity**: High — resource exhaustion / internal SSRF pivot
- **Affected**: Debug proxy deployments
- **Attack vector**: Client opens many CONNECT tunnels to internal services, holds them open

## Fix
- Apply an idle-data timeout to established tunnels (e.g., destroy after N minutes without traffic in either direction)
- Cap concurrent tunnels per client connection
- Restrict CONNECT targets to a configured allowlist

## Reproduction
1. Start the debug proxy
2. Open 1,000 CONNECT tunnels to `169.254.169.254:80` and send no data
3. Tunnels stay open indefinitely; Gateway FD usage grows without bound

## References
- AWS/GCP/Azure metadata service at `169.254.169.254`
- File descriptor exhaustion DoS

`FileDownloader` (new in 9.3, the download half of the deprecated `ImageCopier`) fetches the product `image` and virtual-product `file_url` columns of an import CSV. `downloadUrl()` opened the URL with the raw http stream wrapper (`fopen`), following redirects and validating nothing about the host, so a cell pointing at `http://127.0.0.1/...`, `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/...`, or a public URL that 302-redirects to an internal address was fetched server side. For `file_url` the fetched bytes then become downloadable virtual-product content, turning the import into a read primitive against internal services.

The `ImageCopier` this class replaced ran the same columns through `Tools::copyFromUntrustedSource()`, which rejects private/loopback/link-local hosts, pins the resolved IP against DNS rebinding and re-validates every redirect hop. `FileDownloader` dropped that step. This routes the URL fetch back through it (injected as the `Adapter\Tools` service, the way `ImageCopier` consumes it) and keeps the post-download size cap.

How to test:
- With the fix, an import CSV whose `image` or `file_url` column is `http://127.0.0.1/whatever.jpg` (or `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`) is refused and the row is skipped, instead of PrestaShop fetching it.
- A normal public image/file URL still imports unchanged.
- `php -d date.timezone=UTC vendor/bin/phpunit -c tests/Unit/phpunit.xml tests/Unit/Core/Import/Engine/FileDownloaderTest.php`: the two new `testAUrl…` cases fail on the old `fopen` path and pass with the fix.

## Problem

After #8609, web hosts born from R2 onward have the `soleur-github-app` read token in their credential file, which is rendered into web `hcloud_server.user_data`. Hetzner serves that at `169.254.169.254`. A server-side request forgery in the app, running inside a Docker container, could fetch the token from there.

The git-data host drops metadata access, but its rule (`meta skuid != 0 ip daddr 169.254.169.254 drop`, `cloud-init-git-data.yml`) filters only the host's own OUTPUT path. It does not cover traffic forwarded from Docker containers.

## Scope

- **Forward-path design.** Add an nftables drop of `169.254.169.254` for container traffic, designed to coexist with Docker's firewall chains.
- **Exemptions.** The host's own metadata callers must keep working: `ci-deploy.sh`, `cat-deploy-state.sh`, `inngest-inventory.sh` and `cloud-init-registry.yml` each call the endpoint.
- **Tests.** Mirror git-data's syntax and rehearsal suites: `git-data-nftables-syntax.test.sh` and `git-data-runcmd-rehearsal.test.sh`.
- **Delivery to web-1.** web-1's `user_data` was fixed when the host was created, so the rule has to reach it another way (see #7827).

**Blocking condition:** web-2 must not be promoted to serving traffic until this drop exists.

## Re-evaluate when

The next web-host hardening pass, and before any web-2 promotion.

Related: #8609, #7772 (git-data precedent), #7827.

🚨 **Severity:** CRITICAL
💡 **Vulnerability:** Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF). The application fetched URLs returned by external Cobalt APIs using `requests.get` with default redirect following enabled, without validating the destination IP. This could allow malicious Cobalt instances or crafted redirects to force the server to issue requests to internal network services or cloud metadata endpoints.
🎯 **Impact:** An attacker could bypass external firewalls, interact with internal APIs, or exfiltrate sensitive cloud metadata (e.g., AWS IAM credentials on `169.254.169.254`).
🔧 **Fix:** 
- Implemented `is_safe_url` which resolves the hostname using `socket.getaddrinfo` and rejects any URL pointing to private, loopback, link-local, multicast, or unspecified IP addresses.
- Disabled automatic redirects in the download flow (`allow_redirects=False`) and implemented a manual redirect loop (max 5) that validates each intermediate redirect URL.
- Added explicit cleanup (`response.close()`) for intermediate redirect responses.
✅ **Verification:** Run `python manage.py test` to verify no regressions in the download functionality. Attempting to download from a URL pointing to `http://127.0.0.1` or `http://169.254.169.254` will now fail with a URL validation error.

items.title: Make LM Studio private-network access a user setting instead of a model argument
items.body:
The security scan reported "LM Studio exposes its private-network bypass as a model-controlled argument". `fetch_url` and `research_url` listed `allowPrivate` in their model-visible schemas and passed it straight to the URL and DNS guards. A page the model had just read could ask it to set the flag and reach loopback, RFC1918, link-local or cloud-metadata addresses with a method, headers and body the model chose.

## Changes
- `allowPrivate` is no longer in the `fetch_url` or `research_url` schema.
- Private targets open only through a new per-chat plugin setting, **Allow private network access** (`allowPrivateNetwork`, off by default). It is registered with `ctx.withConfigSchematics` and read from `ctl.getPluginConfig` each time LM Studio builds the tool list. If the config can't be read, private targets stay blocked.
- `fetchUrl(args, opts)` and `researchUrl(args, opts)` now take the setting as a second parameter, separate from the model's arguments. An `allowPrivate` key sent in the arguments is ignored. The SDK's zod parse would also strip it, since it is no longer in the schema.
- Cloud metadata endpoints stay blocked even with the setting on: `169.254.169.254`, `169.254.170.2`, `169.254.170.23`, `169.254.0.23`, `100.100.100.200`, `fd00:ec2::254`, `fd00:ec2::23`, `metadata.google.internal`, `metadata.goog` and `metadata`. This covers IPv4-mapped IPv6 spellings (`[::ffff:169.254.169.254]`), integer and hex IPv4 forms (the URL parser normalises them), DNS answers and every redirect hop. When the setting is on, the DNS lookup now runs anyway so that a hostname resolving to a metadata address is still refused.
- Refusal messages no longer say "set allowPrivate to opt in". They tell the model that the user can turn on the plugin setting.
- Docs: the plugin README has a new "Private network access" section, and the LM Studio guide (`web/docs/lm-studio/`, `web/docs/zh/lm-studio/`) describes the setting instead of `allowPrivate: true`. Both pages are hand-written, not generated.

## Validation
- `cd lmstudio-plugin && npm test` (tsc + `browserTask.test.mjs` + new `privateNetworkSetting.test.mjs`): 19/19 pass.
- New `test/privateNetworkSetting.test.mjs` checks:
  - the setting is registered and defaults to off;
  - neither HTTP tool schema contains `allowPrivate`;
  - a model-sent `allowPrivate: true` cannot reach a loopback HTTP server, and the server sees zero requests;
  - the user setting opens loopback targets to both tools;
  - metadata literals, the mapped-IPv6 and integer spellings, and a redirect from an allowed loopback server to `169.254.169.254` are all refused with the setting on.
- Against main's `src/`, the file fails at import (`readNetworkOptions` doesn't exist there). With that import stubbed, the first three tests fail on main. The "model-sent `allowPrivate` cannot reach a loopback service" test gets `success: true` on main. The metadata tests were not run on main because main would open real connections to those addresses.
- Root `node test/run.js` (part of `test:shard:tail`, which covers the docs pages and plugin README): 2517 passed, 7 failed. The same 7 tests fail on main (74506f078) with the same counts: changelog vs `package.json` version, locale dropdowns, sidepanel streaming, the Providers search box, WebGPU settings, Companion locale keys and `generate_image` wiring. None of them involve the plugin or the LM Studio docs. The other shards don't touch these files and were not run.
- The tests call `fetchUrl`/`researchUrl` and `readNetworkOptions` directly instead of the registered tools' `implementation`. On main, the SDK's `tool()` wrapper parses parameters with its own bundled zod 3.25.76, and the plugin's zod 4.6.6 schemas make it throw `keyValidator._parse is not a function`. That is a pre-existing problem from the zod 4 bump and is not changed here.

## Deploy notes
Users who relied on the model passing `allowPrivate: true` must now turn on **Allow private network access** in the plugin's settings in LM Studio, in each chat that needs localhost or LAN access. Nothing else is needed. The setting is not tested inside a running LM Studio here. Only the SDK config schematics were exercised, with the `{ fields: [{ key, value }] }` config shape the host sends.

items.title: fix: bloqueia IP literal privado no dispatcher e no axios anti-SSRF
items.body:
# What kind of change does this PR introduce?

Correção de segurança (backend/orchestrator, `libraries/nestjs-libraries/src/dtos/webhooks`). `ssrfSafeDispatcher` (undici `Agent`) passa a usar um `connect` próprio (`buildConnector` com o mesmo `ssrfSafeLookup`) que rejeita com `Blocked IP` qualquer host que seja IP literal bloqueado antes de abrir o socket. Os agents http/https de `getSsrfSafeAxios()` ganham a mesma checagem sobrescrevendo `createConnection`. `isBlockedIp` passa a reconhecer IPv4 mapeado em IPv6 na forma hexadecimal (`::ffff:7f00:1`), que é como `new URL()` normaliza `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]`. Hostnames continuam validados pelo `lookup` como antes, hosts e IPs públicos não mudam e `DISABLE_SSRF_PROTECTION=true` continua desligando a proteção em `getSsrfSafeDispatcher()`/`getSsrfSafeAxios()`.

Também traz `jest.config.ts` + `tsconfig.spec.json` (os mesmos da branch `feat/composicoes-api`), porque a configuração na `main` (`getJestProjects()`) não encontrava nenhum projeto e nenhum spec rodava.

# Why was this change needed?

`net.connect`/`tls.connect` não chamam o hook `lookup` quando o host já é um IP literal, então o ramo `net.isIP(hostname)` de `ssrfSafeLookup` nunca rodava. Um `fetch('https://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data', { dispatcher: ssrfSafeDispatcher })` abria a conexão TCP/TLS normalmente. A falha só aparecia depois, como erro de certificado. Rotas com `IsSafeWebhookUrl` no DTO estavam protegidas pela validação estática, mas chamadores que dependem só do dispatcher ficavam expostos, por exemplo:

- `MediaService.uploadFromUrl` via a ferramenta MCP `upload.from.url`, que só valida com zod `.url()`
- `no.auth.integrations.controller.ts`, com `webhookUrl` vindo do redis sem validação
- `post.activity.ts`, com linhas de webhook antigas
- providers com instância customizada (Mastodon custom, WordPress, Lemmy)
- caminhos de mídia em `social.abstract.ts`

O bypass via `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]` / `[::ffff:169.254.169.254]` afetava também `isSafePublicHttpsUrl`, ou seja, também a validação estática dos DTOs.

# Other information:

Revisei todos os usos de `ssrfSafeDispatcher`, `getSsrfSafeDispatcher`, `getSsrfSafeAxios`, `isBlockedIp` e `isSafePublicHttpsUrl`:

- **Hosts públicos fixos** (TikTok, YouTube, Whop, Skool, Reddit, Pinterest, Discord, Dribbble, Tumblr, Moltbook, VK, Bluesky): sem mudança.
- **`connect` em forma de função**: nenhum chamador passa `connectTimeout`, `allowH2`, `socketPath` ou `tls` para esse `Agent`, então os padrões do `buildConnector` são os mesmos de antes.
- **Proxy do axios por variável de ambiente**: para alvos `http://`, um `HTTP_PROXY` configurado como IP literal privado passa a ser bloqueado. Um proxy configurado como hostname que resolve para IP privado já era bloqueado pelo `lookup`, então o comportamento fica consistente. Alvos `https://` via proxy continuam como estavam: o axios troca o agent pelo de túnel.
- **Opt-out ignorado (pré-existente, não alterado)**: `media.service.ts`, `mcp.relay.service.ts`, `local.storage.ts`, `cloudflare.storage.ts` e `public.controller.ts` usam `ssrfSafeDispatcher` direto e por isso ignoram `DISABLE_SSRF_PROTECTION`.

items.title: DeliverHandler POSTs to stored inbox URLs with no scheme or address check
items.body:
## Problem

`DeliverHandler` POSTs signed activities to inbox URLs stored from remote actor documents, using `URLSession.shared` with no address or scheme check (`Sources/DeliverHandler/main.swift:88-98`).

- The inbox and shared-inbox URLs come from whatever a remote actor document says (`KeyManager.swift:95-105`, stored on Follow).
- `URLSession.shared` follows redirects.
- Nothing rejects `http://`, loopback, private (RFC 1918 / ULA), link-local or unspecified addresses.

## Failure scenario

A remote actor whose document gives `inbox: "http://169.254.169.254/latest/..."` follows a FAP account. Every post from that account is then POSTed, signed, to the Lambda's link-local metadata address, or to any internal host a redirect points at.

## Scope

The reply-threading spec (FederatedActivityPublisher#271) hardens remote **fetches** (Step 0 and 0b) and leaves delivery POSTs out. items.title: [security-audit] SSRF bypass to cloud metadata via uncaught IPv4-mapped IPv6 in web proxy guard
items.body:
**Severity:** high

`server.mjs` lines 27-34 (`isPrivateIp`) and 38-50 (`assertSafeTarget`). The guard meant to block private/link-local targets (incl. the `169.254.169.254` cloud-metadata service) only recognizes dotted IPv4 and a few bare IPv6 forms. An IPv4-mapped IPv6 address such as `::ffff:169.254.169.254` contains `.` characters, so it enters the dotted branch where `ip.split('.').map(Number)` yields `[NaN,254,169,254]` and every test (incl. `a>=224`) is false; it then falls through to the IPv6 branch whose regexes (`^::`, `^::1`, `^f[cd]`, `^fe[89ab]`) do not match `::ffff:...`. `isPrivateIp` returns `false`, and `dns.lookup('::ffff:169.254.169.254')` returns the same value, which is also not flagged. The Electron main-process equivalent (`main.cjs` `isLinkLocal`/`embeddedIPv4`) handles this correctly, but the web/browser path does not.

Attack path: anyone who can reach a hosted instance of the web-mode server (BYOK mode, or managed mode with a user-supplied absolute URL, since only relative `/` paths skip the guard) submits `POST /api/proxy` with `{url:"http://[::ffff:169.254.169.254]/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/...", headers:{}, body:''}`. The SSRF guard passes, the server `fetch`es it (IPv4-mapped IPv6 connects to the IPv4 `169.254.169.254`), and the response body (cloud IAM credentials / instance metadata) is returned in the `body` field. The same trick reaches loopback services (`[::ffff:127.0.0.1]`) and LAN hosts behind the server. Fix: strip/parse IPv4-mapped IPv6 in `isPrivateIp` (e.g. first normalize `::ffff:<dotted>` to its IPv4 form and re-check, and also handle `::ffff:a9fe:a9fe` hex form), or have `assertSafeTarget` validate both literal and resolved addresses through a shared IPv6-mapped-aware check.

---

items.title: fix(openapi_plugin): block Azure WireServer and IPv6-embedded private addresses in server URL validation
items.body:
### Description

The OpenAPI plugin server URL validator could be bypassed to reach cloud metadata endpoints in two ways:

1. **Azure WireServer (`168.63.129.16`) is publicly routable.** Unlike the AWS (`169.254.169.254`) and GCP (`metadata.google.internal`) endpoints, the Azure WireServer IP falls in no private range, so `try_categorize_non_public_address` treated it as public and `validate_server_url` allowed it.
2. **IPv4 addresses embedded in IPv6 were classified purely as IPv6.** A link-local or private IPv4 smuggled inside a NAT64 (`64:ff9b::/96`, `64:ff9b:1::/48`), 6to4 (`2002::/16`), or Teredo (`2001::/32`) address looked like a benign public IPv6 address and passed validation.

### Changes

**`152071fe` — WireServer and embedded IPv4**

- Denylist the Azure WireServer endpoint in `_try_classify_ipv4`, and enforce it **even when `allow_private_network_access=True`** — being allowed to reach your own network is not the same as being allowed to reach the host agent's credential endpoint. The private-mode check only inspects literal IP hosts (private mode deliberately does not resolve hostnames).
- Decode IPv4 addresses embedded in IPv6 (`sixtofour`, `teredo`, and the RFC 6052 NAT64 prefixes) in `try_categorize_non_public_address` so the embedded address is classified with the IPv4 rules.
- Add tests covering the WireServer endpoint (literal, DNS-resolved, NAT64- and 6to4-embedded), all three IPv6 embedding forms, and the private-network-access override.

**`0c24fba5` — the remaining metadata endpoints**

The private-mode gate documents that the host agent's cloud metadata endpoint "is always blocked", but it compared the category against `_AZURE_WIRE_SERVER_CATEGORY` only, so every other metadata endpoint passed:

| address | category | before |
|---|---|---|
| `168.63.129.16` | Azure metadata (WireServer) | rejected |
| `169.254.169.254` | link-local | allowed |
| `169.254.170.2` | link-local | allowed |
| `100.100.100.200` | carrier-grade NAT | allowed |
| `fd00:ec2::254` | private (IPv6 ULA) | allowed |

`169.254.169.254` is the IMDS address AWS, GCP and Azure share — the endpoint most SSRF write-ups mean — and `fd00:ec2::254` is its documented IPv6 form.

The category is not a usable signal here. "link-local", "carrier-grade NAT" and "private (IPv6 ULA)" also cover ordinary private addresses that the option exists to permit, so widening the gate to those categories would remove the feature rather than narrow it. The named addresses are matched instead, with IPv4-mapped and NAT64-embedded IPv6 forms resolved to the address they carry first, so `::ffff:169.254.169.254` and `64:ff9b::169.254.169.254` are caught too.

Ordinary private addresses are unaffected:

```
https://10.0.0.5/          allowed
https://172.16.0.1/        allowed
https://192.168.1.50/v1    allowed
https://100.64.0.1/        allowed   <- same category as 100.100.100.200
```

### Test plan

`pytest tests/unit/connectors/openapi_plugin/test_server_url_validator.py` — **72 passed**.

The 10 tests added in `0c24fba5` fail on `152071fe`:

```
6 failed, 66 passed
FAILED ...blocks_cloud_metadata_even_with_private_network_access[https://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/]
FAILED ...[https://169.254.170.2/v2/credentials]
FAILED ...[https://100.100.100.200/latest/meta-data/]
FAILED ...[https://[fd00:ec2::254]/latest/meta-data/]
FAILED ...[https://[::ffff:169.254.169.254]/latest/meta-data/]
FAILED ...[https://[64:ff9b::169.254.169.254]/latest/meta-data/]
```

Fixes #14240

---
