items.title: [SEC-015] Admin-configurable AI base_url allows SSRF
items.body:
## Summary

The AI provider `base_url` is admin-configurable, validated only as a string, and fetched server-side with the upstream response body echoed back to the caller.

## Evidence

`app/Http/Requests/Administrators/UpdateAiSettingsRequest.php:42`

```php
'custom_providers.*.base_url' => ['required_with:custom_providers', 'string', 'max:500'],
```

No scheme restriction, no host allowlist, no private/link-local IP blocking.

`app/Services/Ai/AiModelFetchService.php:132-138`

```php
$endpoint = mb_rtrim($url ?: 'https://api.openai.com/v1', '/').'/models';
$response = Http::timeout(10)->withToken($key)->get($endpoint);
```

`app/Services/Ai/AiModelFetchService.php:397-407` returns the raw upstream body in the error message, so the internal response is exfiltrated to the browser.

`app/Http/Controllers/AiChatController.php:180-190` will even auto-prepend `http://` to a bare host, so plaintext internal calls are trivially configured.

## Impact

A user with `updateAi` sets `base_url` to `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` and clicks "Test connection" / "Fetch models". The server issues the request from inside the VPC and returns the metadata response body. `http://127.0.0.1:6379/` and `http://10.0.0.5:8500/v1/kv` (Consul) are equally reachable.

## Suggested fix

1. Require `https` (or an explicit allowlist of provider hosts).
2. Resolve the host and reject RFC1918 / loopback / link-local / `169.254.169.254` ranges before dispatch.
3. Cap the response size.
4. Never echo the upstream body back to the client — return a generic message and log the detail server-side.

items.title: CloudID key refresh on a stormcos node reaches stormimds, not cloudid (169.254.169.254 is on the node's lo)
items.body:
Found while mining glennswest/stormimds#9 (https://github.com/glennswest/stormimds/issues/9) and the #8 comments (https://github.com/glennswest/stormimds/issues/8#issuecomment-5853052060).

**What happens.** stormd's CloudID key refresh uses `cloudid_url` (`crates/stormd/src/config.rs:388`), which defaults to `169.254.169.254`. It was written against **cloudid**: namespace-owner key resolution, and the `owner` tag. On a stormcos node, though, the stormblock initramfs puts `169.254.169.254/32` on `lo`, and stormimds binds it. Everything in the node's host network namespace, stormd included, reaches **stormimds**, not cloudid. stormimds knows only registered guests, so it answers the node `404 instance not found`, and it has no `public-keys/` route yet (stormimds#5). The refresh gets no keys, and nothing reports why.

stormd#19 changed the refresh to speak IMDSv2 because stormimds refused it. That fix assumed stormimds was the intended server. Which service should answer a node's own processes is still undecided: stormimds#9.

**Latent, not live.** No stormcos golden sets `[ssh] owner` today, so the refresh doesn't run on any node yet.

**Proposed resolution.** Wait for stormimds#9, then either:
- point the stormcos default `cloudid_url` at cloudid explicitly (not the link-local address), if nodes are to be served by cloudid; or
- document that on a node the refresh talks to stormimds, which must then know the node.

Either way, log at `warn!` when the refresh is answered 404, so a shadowed endpoint shows up in the log.

items.title: [MOCA SBX] SSRF guard: resolve once, refuse private and metadata ranges, dial the checked address
items.body:
**Priority: P1** (shape A; in shape B, Cortex must dial the address the front end pinned) · Part of the Cortex × MOCA SBX epic · Not in #905's breakdown · MOCA contract: [MI1 §8.5 item 3](https://github.com/rossoctl/moca/blob/main/docs/specs/2026-09-28-moca-multi-user-isolation-design.md)

## Problem

The proxy runs on the KVM host, next to Redis on `127.0.0.1:6379`, the control plane and cloud metadata at `169.254.169.254`. A sandbox must never reach any of them through the proxy. That includes the DNS-rebinding trick, where a name resolves to a public address for the check and a private one for the dial.

## What Cortex does today

Not found. The only loopback checks are for local process attribution ([`forwardproxy/process.go:249`](https://github.com/rossoctl/cortex/blob/d4394da7997c23ea155bf6a3bb8fec01d91a0069/core/listener/forwardproxy/process.go#L249)) and the transparent proxy's own address ([`transparentproxy/server.go:127`](https://github.com/rossoctl/cortex/blob/d4394da7997c23ea155bf6a3bb8fec01d91a0069/core/listener/transparentproxy/server.go#L127)).

## What MOCA needs

- Resolve the name **once**.
- Refuse loopback, link-local (including `169.254.169.254`), private, unique-local and the host's own addresses → `403 destination_private`.
- Then dial **the address that was checked**.
- The metadata range is refused even if the operator permits private ranges.
- Literal IPs in the request are checked too.

## Design questions

Where in the dial path does this sit for tunnels and for bridged upstream connections alike? Both must dial the same checked address.

## Done when

items.title: Guard scraper against SSRF and fix robots.txt semantics
items.body:
## Problem

**1. SSRF in the inbound-lead webhook.** `POST /webhook/inbound-lead` is unauthenticated and `scrape_homepage` fetched whatever `website` the caller sent (`httpx.AsyncClient(follow_redirects=True)`), with no host checks. Reproduced before this change: I served a page titled `INTERNAL-ADMIN-SECRET` on `http://127.0.0.1:8765/` and sent a lead with that URL. The response came back **200 and contained the internal page title**, and it was also saved to `GET /leads/{id}`. The same path reaches cloud metadata (`http://169.254.169.254/...`) and any internal service, directly or through a redirect.

**2. robots.txt was misread.** `_robots_allows` treated an empty `Disallow:` as `Disallow: /` (`rule = ... or "/"`), so a site with `User-agent: *` / `Disallow:` (which allows everything) was marked "robots.txt disallows this path". It also ignored `Allow:` and matched rules by prefix in file order.

## Fix

- **`src/services/url_guard.py`** (new): allows only `http`/`https` URLs with no embedded credentials. It resolves the host (IP literals are checked directly) and requires **every** returned address to be publicly routable. It rejects loopback, RFC 1918/ULA, link-local (including `169.254.169.254` and `fe80::/10`), CGNAT `100.64/10`, multicast, reserved, and unspecified addresses. It also rejects IPv6 forms that embed a non-public IPv4 address: IPv4-mapped `::ffff:a.b.c.d`, 6to4, Teredo, and NAT64 `64:ff9b::/96`.
- **`guarded_get`** in `scraper.py`: follows redirects **manually** (at most 5) and re-validates every `Location` hop before requesting it. The `robots.txt` fetch goes through the same guard.
- **Byte cap:** the body is streamed and reading stops at `SCRAPE_MAX_BYTES`. Before, the whole page was downloaded and then sliced.
- **`src/services/robots.py`** (new): RFC 9309 rules. It picks the most specific user-agent group and falls back to `*`. The longest match wins, `Allow` wins ties, an empty `Disallow` matches nothing, and `*` and `$` work. `_robots_allows` keeps its signature.
- New setting **`SCRAPE_ALLOW_PRIVATE_HOSTS=false`** (in `.env.example`) turns off the IP check for local development only. The scheme and credential checks still apply. The README "Legal / ToS" section now describes the guard.

## Verification

- `pytest -q`: **58 passed** (was 6). New tests cover 21 non-public IPv4/IPv6 addresses, including metadata and embedded forms, and public addresses being allowed. They also cover hostnames that resolve to private IPs (including a mix of public and private), unresolvable hosts, and `ftp://`, `file://` and `user:pass@` URLs. Two more check that a redirect to `169.254.169.254` is refused **before any request is sent**, plus the redirect limit, the byte cap, and a loopback lead where no request is made. There are 7 robots tests (empty Disallow, longest match, Allow ties, specific group vs `*`, grouped user agents, wildcards and `$`).
- Passes on Python 3.13 locally and **Python 3.12** (the CI version).
- Re-ran the end-to-end reproduction through the FastAPI app. For `http://127.0.0.1:8765/`, `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` and `http://[::1]:8765/` the lead is still scored, but the profile has `scrape_ok=false` with `host '…' resolves to non-public address …`, and nothing is leaked.
- Real public fetches still work: `https://github.com/` and `http://example.com/` scrape fine.

## Known limitation

The check validates DNS and then lets httpx resolve again when it connects, so a DNS-rebinding attacker could in theory race it. Fully closing that needs a transport pinned to the resolved IP, which would be a follow-up if the endpoint is ever exposed publicly. The webhook should also get a shared-secret check before it's deployed.

items.title: HTTP recipes do not block DNS names that resolve to metadata
items.body:
<!-- dedup-key: 82039e60f0ec09625e2d973a5286a8178eddcf6c6b06656fff8327064b1f8fdf -->

## Problem

HTTP recipe fetches check only the URL hostname against link-local and metadata names. A hostname that resolves to a blocked address is still fetched.

`assertRecipeUrlAllowed` parses the interpolated URL and calls `isLinkLocalOrMetadataHost` on `parsed.hostname` only (`app/src/adapters/http/runtime.ts`). Literal forms that the URL parser canonicalizes (`2852039166`, `0xa9fea9fe`, octal dotted quads) become `169.254.169.254` and are rejected. A DNS name such as `169.254.169.254.nip.io` is not in the hostname block list. The fetch then uses `redirect: "manual"` and does not resolve the name first.

The same request can send a minted bearer (`Authorization`) and caller headers such as `Metadata-Flavor`. The response body is stored on the recipe snapshot and can be mapped into service env through `outputs` (for example an `access_token` field). Expose has an `allow_token_body` gate; env interpolation does not.

## Evidence

```ts
function assertRecipeUrlAllowed(name: string, url: string): void {
  let parsed: URL;
  try {
    parsed = new URL(url);
  } catch {
    throw newError(KindConfiguration, `http recipe ${name} request.url is not a valid URL: ${url}`);
  }
  if (isLinkLocalOrMetadataHost(parsed.hostname)) {
    throw newError(KindConfiguration, `http recipe ${name} request.url targets a link-local or metadata host (${parsed.hostname})`);
  }
}
```

## Impact

On a GCE VM, Cloud Workstation, or any host that can reach a cloud metadata service, a `.devctl` recipe can read instance credentials into the supervisor and into service environment. The hostname check looks like that path is closed.

## Attack scenario

A repository's HTTP recipe sets `request.url` to a name the author controls that resolves to `169.254.169.254`, and sets `Metadata-Flavor: Google` (or the AWS IMDSv1 path). `devctl start` runs the recipe, stores the metadata token JSON, and a service env value `${http.<name>.<output>}` receives it. The developer does not have to curl metadata themselves.

## Reproduction

1. On a host that can reach cloud metadata, point an `http:` recipe at a DNS name that resolves to `169.254.169.254` and include the metadata header the cloud requires.
2. Map the credential field in `outputs`.
3. Run `devctl start` and inspect the resolved service env (with reveal). The literal URL `http://169.254.169.254/...` is rejected; the DNS name is not.

## Recommended fix

Resolve the hostname (all A/AAAA answers) before fetch and reject the recipe when any answer is link-local, the metadata IPs already listed in `isLinkLocalOrMetadataHost`, or otherwise disallowed. Re-check on each attempt. Do not follow redirects to those addresses. Apply the same resolved-address check to proxy `upstream.url`, which is not checked today.

## Effort

M

items.title: SSRF guard: unit tests for bad_ip/vet and webhook URL validation, close four bad_ip gaps
items.body:
`crates/instant-server/src/ssrf.rs` guards OAuth discovery/JWKS/token/userinfo fetches and (via `bad_ip`) webhook delivery, and had no tests. This adds a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` there and closes four gaps the tests turned up in `bad_ip`.

## Tests added

**`bad_ip`, table-driven**
- Refused: loopback (`127.0.0.1`, `127.255.255.254`, `::1`), 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, link-local 169.254/16 incl. `169.254.169.254` metadata, `0.0.0.0` and 0/8, broadcast, multicast (`224.0.0.1`, `ff02::1`), CGNAT edges `100.64.0.0` / `100.127.255.255`, `fc00::`/`fd00::`, `fe80::`, `::`, 6to4 `2002::`, Teredo `2001:0::`, NAT64 `64:ff9b::`, and IPv4-mapped `::ffff:127.0.0.1` / `::ffff:10.0.0.1` / `::ffff:169.254.169.254`.
- Allowed: `8.8.8.8`, `1.1.1.1`, `2606:4700:4700::1111`, `2001:4860:4860::8888`, `::ffff:8.8.8.8`, `2001:1::1` (not Teredo), and the addresses just outside each range: `172.15.255.255`, `172.32.0.0`, `100.63.255.255`, `100.128.0.0`, `198.17.255.255`, `198.20.0.0`, `191.255.255.255`, `192.0.1.0`, `223.255.255.255` (just below multicast).

**`vet()` error paths** (`#[tokio::test]`, literal IPs only, no DNS or outbound network)
- Invalid URLs (`not a url`, empty string, `http://`, `https://`) return `Invalid URL: …`. The url crate refuses a special-scheme URL with an empty host at parse time, so that's the path the empty-host case takes.
- `file://`, `ftp://`, `gopher://` and `ws://` return `Unsupported URL scheme: …`, including with `allow_private=true`.
- Private literals are refused with the exact `…does not resolve to a public address.` message: `http://127.0.0.1/`, `http://[::1]:8080/`, `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data`, `http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]/`, `https://10.0.0.1/…`, `http://[fd00::1]/`, `http://0.0.0.0:3000/`, plus the regressions `http://[::127.0.0.1]/` and `http://192.0.0.192/`.
- Public literals are accepted, and `addrs` is pinned to exactly that IP with the right port: 80 for http, 443 for https (implicit and explicit `:443`), an explicit `:8443` is kept, and IPv6 `[2606:4700:4700::1111]` goes to `:443` with brackets stripped from `host`.
- `allow_private=true` returns empty `addrs` and a bracket-stripped `host`.
- Hostname resolution (e.g. `localhost`) is not tested on purpose, since it would depend on the resolver.

## Gaps found in `bad_ip` and fixed (behaviour change)

Each fix is one line in `bad_ip` and has a regression case in `bad_ip_regressions`:

1. **IPv4-compatible `::/96`** (`::127.0.0.1`, `::10.0.0.1`, `::169.254.169.254`). `to_ipv4_mapped()` only unwraps `::ffff:a.b.c.d`, so these got through the guard as "public" IPv6. These addresses are deprecated (RFC 4291), but a stack that honours them (e.g. Linux with the `sit` tunnel up) delivers them to the embedded IPv4 address, loopback included. The whole `::/96` is now refused, `::8.8.8.8` included, because nothing legitimate is served there.
2. **`192.0.0.0/24`** (IETF protocol assignments). This includes DS-Lite `192.0.0.0/29` and `192.0.0.192`, which Oracle Cloud has used as an instance-metadata address.
3. **`198.18.0.0/15`** (benchmarking, RFC 2544). It isn't globally routable, and fake-IP DNS proxies (Clash, Surge) and lab networks hand it out for internal targets.
4. **`240.0.0.0/4`** (reserved class E). It isn't globally routable, and some Kubernetes setups (e.g. GKE) use it for private pod ranges. Previously only `255.255.255.255` within it was caught.

**Left alone:** `2001:db8::/32` (documentation) is never routed, so a fetch there can't reach anything. It stays allowed, and a test records that choice. I also didn't touch other unroutable-but-harmless ranges (IPv4 documentation nets) or `vet`/client behaviour, to keep the change scoped to `bad_ip` gaps that can reach internal hosts.

Legacy `smokescreen.clj` doesn't list these four ranges explicitly, so Rust is now stricter than legacy for them. No parity test exercises these addresses as far as I know.

## Webhook URL validation (`webhooks::assert_valid_url`)

`assert_valid_url` now reads `INSTANT_WEBHOOK_ALLOW_INSECURE` and calls a new private `validate_url(url, insecure_ok)`. Tests call that directly with each mode instead of changing the process environment, which would race with tests running in parallel. Behaviour is unchanged.

The tests use either URLs that are refused before name resolution or literal IPs, so they need no DNS. Each refusal is checked for the full error shape (`validation-failed`, 400, `data-type: webhook`, `input: {url}`, message):
- **https required:** `http://`, `ftp://`, `file://`, `ws://` and unparseable URLs (`not a url`, empty string, `https://`) get "The Webhook url must be https". As in legacy, the scheme check runs first.
- **localhost by name:** `localhost` (including `LOCALHOST:8443`) and `127.0.0.1` get "…localhost is not allowed."
- **Private literal IPs:** `127.0.0.2`, 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, `169.254.169.254`, `0.0.0.0`, CGNAT, multicast, broadcast, and the newly refused `192.0.0.192`, `198.18.0.1` and `240.0.0.1` get "Could not resolve URL."
- **Public literal IPs:** accepted, and `addrs` is pinned to the IP with port 443 by default or an explicit port kept.
- **Insecure mode:** `http://localhost`, `127.0.0.1` and 10/8 are accepted with empty `addrs` (not pinned). Non-http(s) and unparseable URLs still get "Invalid URL."

**Noted, not changed:** for an IPv6 literal, `assert_valid_url` passes the bracketed `host_str()` (`[::1]`) to `IpAddr::parse`. That fails, so the host goes to `lookup_host`, which can't resolve it. Unlike `ssrf::vet`, which strips the brackets, this means every IPv6-literal webhook URL is refused as "Could not resolve URL.", public ones included. That fails closed, so it isn't an SSRF hole, but it's a usability gap. It's left out of this PR, and the tests skip IPv6 literals because that path calls the system resolver.

## Verification

Tests were run **only in GitHub Actions CI**. Nothing was built or tested locally; locally I only ran `cargo fmt`.

### CodeMender Security Fix

**Title**: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in QCodeService via ImageIO.read

**Start Line**: 111

#### Analysis
The `QCodeService` contains a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability due to an insecure use of `ImageIO.read()` with a user-controlled URL. The methods `createGoodShareImage` and `createGrouponShareImage` accept an unvalidated `goodPicUrl` string, which is then passed to the `drawPicture` method. Inside `drawPicture`, this string is directly converted to a `URL` object and passed to `ImageIO.read()`, which triggers an HTTP GET request to the specified URL. An attacker who can control `goodPicUrl` (e.g., when adding or modifying a product or groupon) could supply a URL pointing to an internal service (such as `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` on AWS) or perform port scanning on the internal network.

**Conceptual Exploit Payload:**
An attacker submits a product image URL as `http://127.0.0.1:8080/admin/delete_all` or `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/`. When the system attempts to generate the sharing image (e.g., QR code), the application fetches this URL via `ImageIO.read()`, effectively bypassing the firewall and triggering the SSRF payload from the server's perspective.
